To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Swedish reform of upper secondary education has resulted in an increase of gender gaps in STEM subjects.
the multiple options in Swedish upper-secondary STEM programmes are gendered in ways that may be seen as both a cause and an effect of gendered enrolment patterns.

‘Gendered patterns of enrolment are reproduced in the Swedish upper secondary STEM domain in ways that are not always visible in aggregated data, and that are related to the re-organization into multiple options and the ways gender is articulated in the discourse of choice.’
In summary, our research is concerned with

the ways gender patterns are reproduced in the Swedish educational system through the emergence of multiple choice options, and how this is articulated through the re-organization and differentiation of subject matters.
the ways in which the emergence of multiple choice options in the Swedish upper secondary education system may reproduce gender patterns.
the ways in which gendered patterns are reproduced in relation to processes that are often seen as progressive and beneficial for all students.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Swedish reforms have not resulted in the intended gender equity in STEM.

the introduction of multiple options in Swedish upper-secondary education has not led to a gender-neutral system, neither in terms of the overall distribution of pupils in the different programmes nor in terms of the distribution of boys and girls within the programmes.
multiple options may be a gendered phenomenon, but the extent to which this is the case remains unclear and requires further study.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the multiple options structure is a powerful mechanism that may reproduce gender orders in STEM education.
the multiple options policy has been successful in terms of enrolment and retention rates.
the introduction of multiple options and reorganization of subject matter within Swedish upper secondary education has resulted in an increased number of options for young women and men.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the introduction of multiple options has not resulted in an equal distribution of gendered subjects, but rather has strengthened the reproduction of gender orders in STEM education.
a focus on the multiple options in upper secondary education is needed in order to fully grasp gendered patterns in the STEM domain.
gender orders are reproduced through the re-organization and fragmentation of subject matters and the emergence of multiple choices in upper secondary STEM education.
